title: Effect of nutritional intervention combined with resistance exercise on clinical indicators of patients with sarcopenia in maintenance hemodialysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis

sections.abstract:
This study aims to evaluate the effects of exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention on muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function in maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients with sarcopenia (SP) through a systematic review and meta-analysis.

We searched multiple databases for RCTs published up to November 2024. Inclusion criteria: patients aged ≥18 with end-stage renal disease receiving MHD and diagnosed with SP; experimental group receiving combined exercise and nutrition intervention, and control group receiving either intervention alone; outcome measures including muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function. Meta-analysis was performed using Stata 15.1.

Nine high-quality RCTs involving 513 MHD-SP patients (256 experimental, 257 control) were included. The combined intervention group showed significantly greater improvements in handgrip strength (WMD = 3.78, 95% CI: 2.02–5.53), leg power score (WMD = 5.52, 95% CI: 1.47–9.58), skeletal muscle index (WMD = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.62–1.03), lean body mass (WMD = 2.53, 95% CI: 0.45–4.61), walking speed (WMD = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.01–0.22), 6-minute walk test (WMD = 41.37, 95% CI: 20.16–62.58), and 30-second sit-to-stand test (WMD = 3.37, 95% CI: 1.67–5.07). Heterogeneity analysis showed I 2 ≤ 50% for all outcomes, indicating robust results. Sensitivity and publication bias analyses confirmed the reliability of the findings.

Combined exercise therapy and nutritional intervention significantly improve muscle strength, mass, and physical function in MHD patients with sarcopenia, offering important clinical benefits.
sections.introduction:
End-stage renal disease (ESRD) has become a growing global public health issue, affecting 8% to 16% of the population worldwide [ 1 ]. Hemodialysis (HD) is one of the most commonly used treatments for ESRD, effectively maintaining internal homeostasis and prolonging patient life [ 1 ]. However, the incidence of sarcopenia (SP) significantly increases with age and disease progression in HD patients [ 2 , 3 ]. Sarcopenia is a degenerative syndrome characterized by the progressive decline in skeletal muscle mass and strength, leading to reduced physical fitness and an increased risk of adverse health outcomes, such as falls, fractures, and cardiovascular events [ 2 , 4 , 5 ]. Notably, the prevalence of SP in HD patients is 5 to 10 times higher than in the general population, making it a critical factor affecting both survival and quality of life in these patients [ 3 ].

The pathogenesis of SP in HD patients is multifactorial, including chronic inflammation, metabolic acidosis, protein-energy wasting, and insufficient physical activity [ 6 , 7 ]. Physical inactivity is particularly common among HD patients, with studies showing that about 95% of dialysis patients exhibit reduced activity levels [ 7 , 8 ]. This sedentary behavior exacerbates muscle atrophy and functional decline, further impairing the ability to perform daily activities and worsening overall health [ 6–8 ]. Additionally, nutritional deficiencies are prevalent in HD patients, as they often consume inadequate amounts of protein and energy due to factors like loss of appetite, dietary restrictions, and the catabolic effects of dialysis itself, leading to poor nutritional status [ 9 ].

Exercise therapy, especially resistance training (RE), has emerged as a promising intervention to combat sarcopenia in HD patients. Resistance training stimulates anabolic pathways by applying high-intensity stress to muscles, thereby promoting muscle protein synthesis and significantly improving muscle strength and mass [ 10 , 11 ]. Numerous studies have demonstrated that resistance training significantly enhances muscle strength, physical performance, and quality of life in HD patients [ 10 , 11 ]. Furthermore, nutritional interventions, such as oral nutritional supplements, have been shown to alleviate protein-energy wasting by providing essential nutrients, supporting muscle maintenance, and improving overall nutritional status [ 12 , 13 ].

Both the International Society of Nephrology and the National Kidney Foundation recommend combining exercise therapy with nutritional support in the management of sarcopenia in HD patients [ 14 ]. While these interventions individually have shown significant benefits, the synergistic effects of combining nutritional interventions with resistance training have not been fully explored [ 14 ]. Preliminary studies suggest that the combined use of resistance training and nutritional supplementation may be more effective than either intervention alone in preserving muscle mass and enhancing functional capacity [ 14 ]. However, existing studies show inconsistencies, and there is a lack of large-scale, long-term randomized controlled trials to confirm the effectiveness of combined interventions.

This systematic review and meta-analysis uniquely evaluate the combined effects of nutritional intervention and resistance exercise on clinical indicators of sarcopenia in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (MHD). While previous studies have investigated either exercise or nutritional interventions independently in MHD patients, this meta-analysis distinguishes itself by synthesizing the synergistic effects of both interventions. The novelty of our work lies in its focus on the combined approach, which has the potential to address multiple contributing factors of sarcopenia—such as physical inactivity, protein-energy wasting, and poor nutritional status—in this patient population. Furthermore, our analysis includes studies from diverse healthcare settings and patient populations, strengthening the generalizability and applicability of the findings. By focusing on this combined intervention, our study fills a critical gap in the literature, providing robust evidence to support clinical decision-making and offering practical insights for optimizing treatment strategies in MHD patients with sarcopenia. This contribution is particularly valuable given the growing recognition of sarcopenia as a key determinant of health outcomes in hemodialysis patients and the need for comprehensive management approaches.
sections.methods:
This study aimed to evaluate the clinical effects of exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention in patients with ESRD and SP. The study strictly followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure the scientific rigor and consistency of the included studies [ 15 ]. The inclusion criteria were: randomized controlled trials (RCTs); participants aged ≥18 years, diagnosed with ESRD, receiving regular MHD, and diagnosed with sarcopenia; the experimental group received exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention, while the control group received either exercise therapy or nutritional intervention alone. The primary outcome measures included at least one of the following: muscle strength, muscle mass, or physical function. The exclusion criteria were: studies where the full text was unavailable; duplicate publications, reviews, meta-analyses, or conference abstracts; non-Chinese or non-English literature; studies involving patients receiving irregular hemodialysis; and studies without a control group or incomplete pre- and post-treatment data.

The literature search was performed using a computer-based method, with extensive searches conducted across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data. The search period was from the establishment of each database to November 2024. The search strategy combined MeSH terms and free-text keywords such as “hemodialysis,” “sarcopenia,” “nutrition intervention,” and “resistance exercise,” using Boolean operators (“AND,” “OR”) to ensure comprehensive and relevant results. Detailed search strategy in different databases were provided in supplemental material 1 . Additional searches were conducted through reference lists, conference proceedings, and dissertations to minimize the risk of missing relevant studies.

During the literature screening process, the search results were de-duplicated using EndNote 21 software. Two independent researchers then screened the titles and abstracts according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, removing studies that clearly did not meet the requirements. Full texts of the remaining studies were reviewed to confirm their eligibility. Any disagreements between the researchers were resolved through discussion or by involving a third researcher to ensure consistency and accuracy in the selection process.

Data extraction was conducted by one researcher and verified by a second researcher. A standardized data extraction form was used to collect the following information: study characteristics (e.g. author, publication year, country), sample characteristics (e.g. sample size, patient age, sex ratio, disease duration), intervention details (e.g. specifics of exercise therapy and nutritional intervention, intervention duration and frequency), and primary outcomes (e.g. methods and results of muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function measurements).

The quality of the included studies was assessed by two researchers following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews, evaluating seven aspects: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other biases [ 16 ]. Based on these evaluations, studies were classified into three quality levels: A (low risk of bias in all areas), B (low risk of bias in some areas), and C (high risk of bias). Studies rated as C were excluded. Any disagreements during the quality assessment process were resolved through discussion or by involving a third researcher to ensure consistency and accuracy.

Meta-analysis was conducted using Stata 15.1 software [ 17 , 18 ]. First, heterogeneity across studies was assessed using the chi-square test (χ 2 test) and I 2 statistic. If p ≥ 0.1 and I 2 ≤50%, the studies were considered homogeneous, and a fixed-effect model was applied. If p < 0.1 and I 2 >50%, the studies were considered heterogeneous, and a random-effects model was used. For outcome measures, weighted mean difference (WMD) was used when the same measurement tools were employed. If different measurement tools were used, standardized mean difference (SMD) was applied. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05, and effect sizes were expressed as 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Sensitivity analysis was performed using Duval and Tweedie’s trim and fill method to assess the stability of the meta-analysis results and to determine whether the effect size was significantly influenced by studies with small sample sizes [ 19 ]. Publication bias was evaluated using Egger’s regression test when five or more studies were included [ 20 ]. Through these statistical methods, the study aimed to comprehensively assess the clinical effects of exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention on patients with maintenance hemodialysis and sarcopenia, providing scientific evidence to inform clinical decision-making.
sections.results:
According to the predefined search strategy, a total of 1,067 relevant articles were retrieved from major databases: 1,052 from the databases and 15 through supplementary reference searches. After removing duplicates, 886 articles remained. These were further screened by reviewing titles and abstracts, resulting in the exclusion of 875 articles due to low applicability. The excluded articles included those that did not meet the study criteria (794), conference abstracts [ 7 ], animal studies [ 21 ], articles without full text access [ 5 ], and reviews [ 22 ]. Two studies, which could not provide extractable data for valid meta-analysis, were excluded after full-text evaluation. Ultimately, 9 studies met the inclusion criteria (see Table 1 ), and the search process is shown in Figure 1 [ 23–31 ].

Flow diagram of literature screening process.

Baseline characteristics of included studies for meta-analysis.

RT, Resistance Training; Protein Supplementation, Dietary protein or supplements to increase muscle mass or strength; 6MWT, 6-min walk test; HGS, Handgrip strength; SMI, Skeletal muscle index; LBM, Lean body mass; LPS, Leg press strength; GS, Gait speed; 30s-STS, 30-s sit-to-stand test.

The 9 included studies were all RCTs conducted in five countries: China (1), the United States (3), Brazil (2), Indonesia (1), and Mexico (2), published between 2007 and 2020. These studies enrolled a total of 513 patients with HD-SP, with 256 in the experimental group and 257 in the control group. The design of these studies compared exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention to either exercise therapy or nutritional intervention alone. The intervention period ranged from 12 weeks to 2 years, with intervention frequency ranging from 2 to 3 times per week. The interventions primarily involved upper limb dumbbell exercises, lower limb weight training, ankle joint weight lifting, and aerobic exercises (e.g. cycling), with some studies also incorporating oral nutritional supplements. The primary outcome measures included muscle strength (e.g. grip strength), muscle mass (e.g. skeletal muscle index, lean body mass), and physical function (e.g. 6-min walking test, 30-s sit-to-stand test, gait speed, etc.) ( Table 1 ) [ 23–31 ].

The quality and risk of bias assessment of the included studies indicated that most studies had high quality and low risk of bias ( Figure 2(A) and (B) ) [ 23–31 ]. Specifically, all studies employed random allocation, and most studies performed well in terms of allocation concealment, and outcome measurement blinding.

Risk-of-bias assessment for included RCTs: A. Risk of bias summary, B. Risk of bias graph.
sections.discussion:
This meta-analysis combined nine randomized controlled trials involving 513 patients undergoing MHD with sarcopenia (SP) to assess the effects of exercise therapy combined with nutritional interventions on muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function. The analysis revealed that the combined intervention group showed significantly better outcomes than the control group (exercise therapy alone or nutritional intervention alone) in terms of handgrip strength (HGS), leg power score (LPS), skeletal muscle index (SMI), lean body mass (LBM), gait speed (GS), 6-min walk test (6MWT), and 30-s sit-to-stand test (30s-STS). These results not only confirm the effectiveness of exercise therapy and nutritional intervention in improving muscle and functional status in MHD-SP patients but also highlight the synergistic effects of combining both interventions.

Compared to previous studies, the positive effects observed in this study are highly consistent with the findings of Johansen et al. who similarly reported significant improvements in muscle strength with resistance training for both upper and lower limbs [ 24 , 32 ]. These consistent results support the effectiveness of resistance training in improving muscle strength in hemodialysis patients. Additionally, Rosa et al. observed an increase in muscle strength following 30 min of resistance training, although they did not find significant changes in muscle reserve indicators [ 25 ]. Together, these studies indicate that resistance training has a universally positive effect on improving muscle strength in hemodialysis patients.

However, there are some notable differences between this study and previous research, particularly in terms of the nutritional status of the study population. The average body mass index (BMI) in our study was 21.5 ± 3 kg/m 2 , significantly lower than the approximately 27 kg/m 2 reported by Cheema et al. and Johansen et al. This suggests a higher prevalence of malnutrition in our population, with 83.6% of patients affected [ 33 , 34 ]. The low BMI and inadequate caloric intake (mean 24.2 ± 11 kcal/kg/day) may be key factors contributing to high protein energy wasting [ 35 ]. Unlike other studies with better-nourished participants, our population faced significant nutritional challenges due to long-term dialysis and dietary restrictions. This malnutrition not only exacerbates muscle wasting and functional decline but also increases the risk of cardiovascular events and infections. Therefore, in malnourished MHD patients, combined exercise and nutritional interventions are particularly critical. Nutritional interventions support muscle repair and growth by providing essential protein and energy, while resistance training enhances muscle strength and mass. Together, they complement each other to improve overall health [ 14 ].

It is important to note that the interventions employed in the studies included in our meta-analysis were not uniform. For instance, there were variations in the types of exercise used, with some studies incorporating aerobic components alongside resistance training. While all studies included resistance exercises, the specific modalities, intensity, and duration of these exercises varied. Some studies used weight training for both upper and lower limbs, while others incorporated exercises using machines or bodyweight resistance. The inclusion of aerobic exercise, such as cycling or walking, in some protocols likely influenced the physical function outcomes (e.g. 6MWT and gait speed) differently compared to studies focusing strictly on resistance training. These differences in exercise protocols may have contributed to the variability in the outcomes observed, particularly for physical function measures.

Similarly, the nutritional interventions varied across studies. The source of protein (e.g. plant-based versus animal-based), the caloric content, and the specific nutritional supplementation (e.g. oral nutritional supplements versus dietary modifications) differed. Such variability in supplementation could have contributed to differing outcomes in muscle mass and strength. The heterogeneity in these two key intervention components—exercise types and nutritional strategies—should be considered when interpreting the results of this meta-analysis. Standardization of these intervention components in future studies would help reduce variability and allow for clearer conclusions.

Patients on MHD often experience reduced physical activity, with approximately 95% of dialysis patients showing decreased activity levels. This sedentary behavior not only leads to muscle atrophy and functional decline but also negatively affects cardiorespiratory function, further impairing patients’ ability to perform daily activities and diminishing their quality of life [ 21 ]. Our study showed a significant decline in muscle strength in the control group, aligning with the negative effects of sedentary behavior on muscle health. In contrast, patients who received the combined intervention not only experienced significant improvements in muscle strength but also showed enhanced physical function, including GS and 6MWT. These findings suggest that exercise therapy not only improves muscle strength and mass but also boosts overall health and quality of life by enhancing cardiorespiratory function and activity endurance. Improved cardiorespiratory function can enhance oxygen uptake and utilization, increasing patients’ activity endurance, enabling them to perform daily activities more easily, reducing fatigue, and ultimately improving life satisfaction.

Additionally, exercise therapy may have a positive impact on sleep quality. Although this study did not assess sleep quality, previous research has shown that exercise can reduce sleep disturbances in dialysis patients, thereby improving their quality of life [ 22 ]. Regular exercise can regulate the body’s internal clock, promote deep sleep, improve sleep efficiency, and reduce sleep onset latency and nighttime awakenings [ 22 , 36 , 37 ]. Improved sleep quality not only enhances daily living but may also further promote overall health by reducing stress levels and inflammatory responses [ 37 ]. Therefore, future studies should consider sleep quality as a key outcome to comprehensively assess the multifaceted effects of exercise interventions on the quality of life of MHD patients.

It is important to note that the exercise intervention in this study was safe, with no exercise-related adverse events reported. This finding has significant implications for clinical practice, indicating that the combination of resistance training and nutritional intervention is both safe and feasible when conducted under strict monitoring and personalized guidance. This result strongly supports the broader implementation of such interventions in clinical settings, especially in resource-limited environments where patient adherence may be lower. Safety is a critical factor in determining whether any intervention can be widely applied. The findings of this study suggest that the combined intervention is not only effective but does not pose additional health risks to patients, thereby laying a solid foundation for future clinical applications.

Taken together, this study, through a rigorous systematic review and meta-analysis, confirms the significant benefits of combining exercise therapy with nutritional intervention to improve muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function in patients with MHD and sarcopenia. Despite limitations such as variations in the nutritional status of the study population, the combined intervention demonstrates substantial clinical potential. Future research should investigate the long-term effects of different intervention intensities and durations on MHD-SP patients, as well as validate these effects in larger and more diverse patient populations. Furthermore, developing personalized, sustainable intervention programs that consider individual patient needs and circumstances could enhance the effectiveness of interventions and improve patient adherence, leading to better clinical outcomes. These efforts will provide a more solid scientific basis for optimizing the management of sarcopenia in MHD-SP patients, potentially improving both their quality of life and survival rates.

A key strength of this study lies in its strict adherence to PRISMA guidelines and the use of systematic review and meta-analysis methodologies. By synthesizing multiple high-quality RCTs, this approach has enhanced the reliability and generalizability of the conclusions. Moreover, this study evaluated various indicators, including muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function, to comprehensively assess the clinical effects of the combined intervention. Sensitivity analysis and publication bias detection were also conducted, ensuring the robustness of the meta-analysis results and confirming the absence of significant bias. The wide geographic coverage of the studies included, which spanned China, the United States, Brazil, Indonesia, and Mexico, further strengthens the external validity and applicability of the findings.

However, this study has several limitations. First, although the overall heterogeneity was low, differences in intervention methods, durations, and measurement tools across the included studies may have impacted the consistency of the results. Second, some studies involved interventions of lower intensity or shorter duration, which may not have fully captured the potential benefits of more intensive or long-term interventions. Additionally, while this meta-analysis included a relatively large number of studies, the sample sizes of individual studies were limited, which may have reduced the statistical power of certain outcome measures. Another important limitation is the cultural and geographical variability among the study populations. Differences in healthcare environments and lifestyles across countries could influence both the implementation and the effectiveness of the intervention. Finally, the absence of long-term follow-up in some studies restricts our understanding of the lasting effects of the combined intervention on sarcopenia and related health outcomes.
sections.conclusion: The results of this meta-analysis show that exercise therapy combined with nutritional intervention significantly improves muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis with sarcopenia. Developing personalized and sustainable intervention programs that take into account the individual needs and circumstances of patients can enhance the effectiveness of these interventions and improve patient adherence, ultimately leading to better clinical outcomes.
